title: Sonar-TS: Search-Then-Verify for Time Series Databases
one_liner: When you ask a database a question about shapes in time series, split the search into two steps: fast SQL to find candidate windows, then Python code to verify which ones really match.
lead: Imagine searching for a pattern in years of stock prices: you want to find all the times the price rose quickly, then fell. A regular database can find numbers, but it cannot understand shapes like "rapid rise then fall." A machine-learning model could understand the shape, but it cannot read billions of data points without running out of memory. Sonar-TS splits the job: SQL finds candidate windows using pre-computed summaries, then Python code checks which ones truly match the shape you described.

problem.h2: Two worlds that do not talk
paras: Databases are fast at finding numbers: "Which rows have temperature above 80?" But they cannot understand continuous shapes. Ask a database to find "periods when temperature spiked then plateaued" and it fails, because shapes live in signals, not in individual rows.

Machine-learning models understand shapes perfectly. Feed them years of stock prices and they spot patterns instantly. But these models have a hidden memory limit (called context length): they can only ingest a few thousand data points at a time. Real databases store millions or billions of points. A model cannot swallow them all.

A beginner tries one of two things: (1) Pass the entire history to a model and watch it run out of memory, or (2) Use SQL alone and admit it cannot understand the shape you want. Sonar-TS refuses both.

callout.html: Use SQL to fast-scan pre-made summaries and find candidate windows, then use Python to verify each candidate against the raw signal.

panels.title: 1. The problem: two tools, zero overlap
panels.viz_args: SQL finds numbers, ML understands shapes. Neither does both.
panels.caption: SQL is fast but dumb to shapes. ML is smart but chokes on billions of points.

panels.title: 2. Search step: SQL pings summaries via feature index
panels.caption: Pre-computed features (SAX codes, trends, slopes) let SQL quickly sift millions of windows without loading raw data.

panels.title: 3. Verify step: Python locks onto each candidate
panels.caption: Only the candidates SQL found get loaded and checked by Python code against the actual raw signal.

panels.title: 4. The payoff: fast + accurate
panels.viz_args: SQL found 200, Python verified 17 are right
panels.caption: No memory blown, no patterns missed, no false positives.

panels.title: 5. The result: complex queries work
panels.caption: Users ask for patterns. The system returns the exact timestamps and values that match.

steps.text: In English: find times when temperature rose fast then stayed flat.
The model breaks the question into steps: detect the rise, detect the plateau, verify both happened in order.
SQL queries the feature index (pre-made summaries) to fetch windows where the trend matches roughly.
For each candidate window, Python computes the real slope and flatness of the raw signal.
Only windows where both the rough pattern (SQL) and the precise shape (Python) match are returned to the user.

paras: Sonar-TS changes WHERE the query plan executes: instead of trying to do all the work in one place (either SQL or a model), it splits the work. SQL handles coarse-grained filtering on summaries; Python handles fine-grained verification on raw data. This split is the engine of the whole system.

hidden.name: candidate window pool
paras: The hidden quantity is how many windows pass the SQL filter before verification begins. If the feature index (SAX codes, trend slopes, etc.) finds 10,000 candidates out of a billion possible windows, the verification step only has to check 10,000, not a billion. The tighter the SQL filter, the fewer candidates Python has to verify. Fewer candidates means the system finishes faster because Python loads and checks less data, and the overall latency is dominated by that verification cost.

Sonar-TS estimates this by building a multi-scale feature index offline. Each window in the database gets a SAX code (a short letter sequence that captures the shape roughly) and other summaries. At query time, SQL uses fuzzy regex matching against these summaries to find candidates. The paper shows that a good feature index cuts the search space from billions to hundreds or thousands, making verification tractable.

heat.caption: Darker: SQL filtering and Python verification together control how many windows pass, how fast, and how accurate the final result is.

reads.html: Imagine sifting through a billion grains of sand looking for red ones. You cannot check each grain by hand. Instead, you have a coarse sieve (SQL) that catches the ones that might be red, then human eyes (Python) that confirm each caught grain is truly red.

The feature index maps each time series window to a SAX representation and trend summary. SQL fuzzy matches against these summaries (searching for patterns like ab*de*ab in regex form). Candidates are then verified via generated Python code that computes exact metrics on raw signals.

mechanism.h2: Why splitting search and verify fixes the problem
paras: The problem is a bottleneck: databases are small but dumb (cannot see shapes), models are smart but huge (cannot hold all data). Splitting work unblocks both.

SQL search runs on summaries, not raw data. Summaries are tiny (a few numbers per window), so SQL scans billions of windows in seconds without memory pressure. It finds rough candidates. Some candidates are false alarms because summaries are coarse.

Python verify loads only the candidates SQL found, not the whole database. Python computes the exact shape metrics (slope, plateau length, etc.) on raw data. It catches false alarms and confirms true matches. This two-step approach guarantees: (1) no patterns are missed (SQL recall is high because feature index is comprehensive), (2) false alarms are caught (Python precision is high because it checks real data), and (3) the system never loads more data than it can hold in memory (because verification only touches candidate windows, not the whole history).

stages.s: Billions of time series points, natural language query, feature index
LLM planner decomposes the query into sub-steps
SQL generates fuzzy regex against SAX summaries
SQL executes, returns rough candidate windows
Python generated code loads candidates and computes exact metrics
Filters to windows where raw signal matches the query
Precise timestamps and values of matching windows

math.words: Each window w receives a relevance score from SQL based on how well its SAX code and trend summary match the query pattern; only windows scoring above a threshold pass to Python for verification.
math.equation: S_SQL(w) = count_matches(sax_code(w), query_pattern_regex) + trend_match_bonus(w) if S_SQL(w) >= threshold_SQL then verify(w) else discard(w)
symbols: SQL relevance score for window w
SAX letter sequence of window w (e.g. abcde)
pattern to match in SQL (e.g. a+.*b+)
extra points if slope, plateau, or direction matches
minimum score to pass to Python verification

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose SQL searches for pattern 'rise then plateau' in SAX codes.
Window A: SAX code aabbc, matches regex a+b+c = 2 matches + trend bonus 1 = score 3.
Window B: SAX code cccaa, matches regex a+b+c = 1 match + trend bonus 0 = score 1.
Threshold is 2. Window A passes to Python verification (score 3 >= 2), Window B is discarded (score 1 < 2).
Python then confirms: Window A's raw signal truly rises then plateaus. Match found.

math.note: SQL filters coarsely on summaries; Python verifies precisely on raw data. The threshold trades speed: lower threshold brings more candidates and slower verification, higher threshold risks missing matches.

charts.title: Naive approach: use SQL alone
charts.note: SQL alone cannot express morphological patterns. Users get wrong or no results.

charts.title: Naive approach: use model alone
charts.note: Models understand shapes but run out of memory on real databases.

charts.title: Sonar-TS: search-then-verify
charts.note: Sonar-TS balances semantic precision with scalability. It handles complex queries that traditional methods fail on.

items.html: If the SAX codes or trend summaries do not capture the pattern you care about, SQL will miss candidates entirely. The query will return no results even though the pattern exists. Example: if your database only stores average slope per window but you need to detect sudden spikes, the index is too coarse.

Building and storing a feature index for billions of windows takes storage and offline compute time. If the database changes constantly, the index becomes stale. Trading off index freshness against query accuracy is a real tension.

If SQL returns 100,000 candidates and Python has to load and verify each one against raw data, the verify step becomes a bottleneck. The system is fast only when SQL filters aggressively. Poorly written query plans lead to huge candidate pools.

Build the feature index carefully so it captures the shapes users actually ask about. Write good query plans so the LLM planner decomposes queries into verifiable sub-steps. Then Search-Then-Verify is fast and accurate, because SQL does the cheap sifting and Python does only the necessary precise checking.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small time series database with 100,000 synthetic data points (e.g., randomly walking prices). Include a feature index (SAX codes and trend summaries pre-computed for all windows). Write a query: 'Find all times when price rose more than 5% then stayed flat for at least 10 steps.' Generate SQL to search the feature index and return candidates. Write Python code to verify each candidate (compute real slope and flatness on raw data). Count: how many SQL candidates? How many Python verifications passed? Time both steps separately.
demo.closing: The demo must show that SQL eliminates the need to scan all 100,000 windows, and Python eliminates false alarms that SQL caught. That is the whole system: fast coarse search, then precise fine-grained check.
